topicName: Lucene Underlying Storage and Inverted Index
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Lucene Underlying Storage and Inverted Index in Elasticsearch"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Elasticsearch is fundamentally built on top of Apache Lucene, a high-performance, full-featured text search engine library. Understanding how Lucene manages underlying storage and constructs the inverted index is essential for optimizing query performance and managing cluster resources effectively."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The Anatomy of an Inverted Index"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Traditional databases store data row by row, making full-text searches across large datasets extremely slow. Lucene solves this by using an inverted index. Instead of mapping documents to words, it maps words (terms) to the documents containing them."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Term Dictionary: A sorted list of unique terms extracted from the text fields during analysis."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Posting List: A list of document IDs that contain the specific term, along with metadata such as term frequency, positions, and offsets."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Term Index: A memory-resident prefix tree (or FST - Finite State Transducer) that points to blocks within the on-disk Term Dictionary."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Lucene Segments and Immutability"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"An Elasticsearch shard is comprised of multiple Lucene segments. A segment is an independent, self-contained inverted index. Crucially, Lucene segments are immutable. Once written to disk, a segment cannot be modified."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Updates: Handled as a delete followed by an add. The old document is marked as deleted via a .del bitset file, and a new document is written to the latest segment."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Deletions: Soft-deletes are tracked in a deletion file. Space is only reclaimed during segment merging."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Underlying File Structure"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"On the filesystem, a Lucene segment consists of numerous files with different extensions. Each file serves a specific low-level purpose in data retrieval."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":".tim - Term Dictionary (contains terms and stats)
.tip - Term Index (FST loaded into RAM for fast lookups)
.doc - Posting List (document IDs and term frequencies)
.pos - Positions (term positions for phrase queries)
.fdt - Stored Fields (original document source data)"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Segment Merging and Background Maintenance"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Because every write creates a new segment, the number of segments can grow rapidly, consuming file descriptors and memory. Elasticsearch runs a background process called the Merge Policy that periodically combines smaller segments into larger ones."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"During a merge, deleted documents are permanently purged, freeing up physical disk space."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Merged segments are written to disk as a single new segment, and the old segments are subsequently unlinked and deleted."},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"By leveraging immutable segments, memory-mapped FSTs for term lookups, and efficient posting lists, Lucene delivers exceptional search speeds. Understanding these internal mechanics allows engineers to design better mappings, tune refresh intervals, and manage segment merging policies for optimal performance."}]
